action_criteria.expected_evidence: 3.4 cm right temporoparietal ring-enhancing mass with thick, irregular, nodular rim and central necrosis, restricted diffusion along the rim with facilitated diffusion centrally (no central restriction), extensive edema and 5 mm leftward midline shift, single lesion
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, SWI, post-contrast T1) to characterize the ring-enhancing right temporal-parietal lesion, its diffusion pattern and its mass effect
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with diffusion characterizes the ring-enhancing lesion as far as imaging can (rim versus central restriction, wall morphology), defines the mass effect that governs lumbar puncture safety, and plans the approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Markedly elevated rCBV (ratio 3.1) in the nodular enhancing rim with low core rCBV and mildly elevated perilesional rCBV
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion MRI) to assess rCBV in the enhancing rim and target the biopsy
action_criteria.rationale: A markedly hyperperfused rim supports a high-grade neoplasm and points the biopsy to the most vascular nodular rim; it does not exclude abscess, and the diagnosis remains tissue-based.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Rim Cho/NAA 4.8 with lipid-lactate and no acetate, succinate or alanine peaks
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterize the metabolite profile of the rim and core
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated choline without amino acid peaks supports a neoplasm over pyogenic abscess; it does not establish the entity.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial primary malignancy or lymphadenopathy identified; supports primary brain tumor over metastasis

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4, with IDH1 R132H negative (no IDH mutation on sequencing), ATRX retained, MGMT unmethylated, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification and +7/-10
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by stereotactic aspiration and biopsy of the right temporoparietal lesion with frozen section, the aspirate going to microbiology, or by resection, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation; aspiration comes first because abscess remains possible and aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic
action_criteria.rationale: Aspiration with frozen section and culture settles abscess against tumour; once tumour is confirmed, surgery should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.rationale: Gram stain and culture of the aspirate are the microbiological test of a brain abscess; with the histology they decide between abscess and necrotic tumour (ESCMID 2024).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start empirical antibiotics for a presumed abscess before the stereotactic aspirate is taken while he remains stable and the procedure can be done within about 24 hours (ESCMID 2024): antibiotics lower the culture yield and do not replace tissue.
Do not perform a lumbar puncture with 5 mm midline shift: the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (radiotherapy, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not drain the lesion as a presumed abscess without frozen section and histology of its wall: aspiration alone risks missing a neoplasm.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Weigh the MRI diffusion pattern (restriction along the rim, not centrally), the rim rCBV of 3.1 and the absence of amino acid peaks on spectroscopy: together they support a high-grade neoplasm over abscess, but tissue with microbiology decides.

Refer urgently to neurosurgery for stereotactic aspiration and biopsy of the right temporoparietal lesion with frozen section, Gram stain and culture, proceeding to maximal safe resection once tumour is confirmed; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Monitor capillary glucose on dexamethasone in this patient with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.8%); expect to need insulin because metformin and glipizide are unlikely to suffice, and reduce the glucose-lowering treatment as the steroid is tapered.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; at age 55 with KPS 80, the standard for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), noting that the unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts less benefit from temozolomide.

key_clinical_evidence: Diffusion: pyogenic abscess typically restricts centrally within the pus cavity, whereas a necrotic high-grade glioma restricts along the hypercellular rim with facilitated diffusion centrally; this lesion shows rim restriction without central restriction, which favours tumour

Perfusion: a hyperperfused rim (rCBV 3.1) reflects tumour neovascularity and favours neoplasm over abscess, whose rim is reactive tissue; it supports and targets the biopsy but does not exclude abscess
Spectroscopy: abscess cavities often show acetate, succinate or alanine peaks from bacterial metabolism; their absence with high choline at the rim favours neoplasm

Low-grade fever, mildly raised CRP and ESR and a recent dental procedure anchor toward abscess; normal WBC and procalcitonin and negative blood cultures weaken it, and the aspirate and histology settle it
A thick, irregular, nodular rim favours neoplasm; abscess walls are usually thin and smooth, often thinner medially
When abscess remains possible, stereotactic aspiration with frozen section, Gram stain and culture comes first and is followed by maximal safe resection once tumour is confirmed

metadata.diagnostic_challenge_notes: This is the first GBM-vs-abscess ring-enhancement diagnostic puzzle in the GLIO-HG set. The case tests whether the agent correctly interprets the DWI pattern (peripheral vs. central restriction), orders and integrates MR perfusion (high rCBV favours tumour) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho without amino acid peaks favours tumour), and resists premature closure on the abscess diagnosis despite three embedded red herrings (low-grade fever, recent dental procedure with peri-apical inflammation, and mildly elevated CRP/ESR). The emergency physician's impression of 'abscess more likely' is a deliberate anchoring cue that a competent agent must override via systematic imaging interpretation.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required criteria (MRI, labs, performance status, tissue, aspirate Gram stain and culture), recommended perfusion, spectroscopy and blood cultures, 3 red herrings (fever, dental history, inflammatory markers); imaging favours tumour over abscess but aspiration with frozen section and culture settles it; the emergency physician's 'abscess more likely' is an anchoring cue

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 55-year-old right-handed South Asian male, a mathematics teacher, who presents with a 3-week history of progressive right-sided pulsatile headache, left arm weakness, and mild difficulty with calculations and word retrieval. He initially attributed the headache to stress and fatigue following a dental crown replacement procedure performed on his lower right first molar 3 weeks ago under local anesthesia. At that visit, the dentist noted mild peri-apical inflammation on pre-procedure radiograph, which was treated with the crown; the patient completed a 5-day prophylactic course of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily post-procedure (completed approximately 2 weeks ago). His wife first noticed left arm clumsiness about 2 weeks ago when he kept dropping objects, and more recently he has had episodes of forgetting students' names and making arithmetic errors on the blackboard, which is completely out of character. He describes the headache as progressively worsening, worse in the morning and when bending forward, different in quality from any previous headaches, and not fully relieved by acetaminophen. He has had no seizures, no loss of consciousness, no fever at home (family noted 'he felt warm' on one occasion last week), no nausea or vomiting, no neck stiffness, and no rash. He denies weight loss, night sweats, or known exposure to sick contacts. On arrival to the emergency department, a non-contrast CT head was performed and revealed a hypodense lesion in the right temporal-parietal region with surrounding edema and 5 mm leftward midline shift, prompting urgent neurology admission and MRI. Given the recent dental procedure with documented peri-apical inflammation, the emergency physician charted an impression of 'right temporoparietal lesion with edema: brain abscess vs. neoplasm, abscess more likely given dental source.'
